Project: PRJ-BASALT
Type: Client deliverable
Date: 2026-02-20

PROJECT BASALT — Reputational due diligence on Aurora Offshore Energia SA and its founder | Source Report | Prepared for client use only

**Key findings**

- Aurora Offshore Energia's founder is credited by all four sources with genuine technical credibility in deepwater subsea tie-backs, but three of four describe a centralised decision-making culture in which commercial commitments are made verbally and documented late, if at all.
- Two sources independently describe a — undisclosed 2021 lifting incident on the Serra Azul-chartered support vessel that was reported internally as a "near miss" but which Source A believes met the threshold for external notification.
- Regulatory relationships are characterised as correct rather than captured; Source C states the company has twice been placed under enhanced monitoring for late environmental filings but has never been subject to a formal sanction proceeding.
- Procurement integrity is the weakest area: Source D describes a sole-source award pattern favouring two intermediary suppliers, one of which Source A links to a person previously employed by the founder.
- No source alleges criminal conduct, and none is aware of any investigation by Ministério Público Federal touching the company or its officers.

**Sources consulted**

- **Source A** — a former senior operating executive of the target with direct line responsibility for offshore assets and vendor management until his departure; strong historical access, diminishing currency.
- **Source B** — a serving regulatory affairs executive at the target with sight of filings, inspection correspondence and incident logs; excellent current access, institutionally loyal.
- **Source C** — a senior official in the Brazilian federal energy ministry with oversight of the upstream licensing and compliance interface; authoritative on the regulatory record, distant from commercial detail.
- **Source D** — a procurement lead at a large mining counterparty that has tendered alongside and against the target; good visibility of bidding conduct in shared supply markets.

---

**1. Founder profile and management culture**

Source A, who reported to the founder for four years, describes him as an engineer by formation who "has never stopped being the chief engineer". Source A says the founder personally reviewed well design decisions long after the company had grown beyond the point where that was practical, and that this produced both unusually strong technical outcomes and a chronic bottleneck. Source A adds that the founder's authority was reinforced by the presence of his son-in-law as head of the chartering desk, an arrangement Source A says was never disclosed to the board's audit committee in the period he was present.

Source B, speaking from a current vantage point, offers a more measured characterisation. She describes the founder as demanding but says he has since 2022 delegated substantially more to a professionalised executive committee, and that the chartering desk is now headed by an external hire. Source B nonetheless confirms that significant commercial undertakings are still frequently agreed by the founder in person before the legal function is engaged, and says her own department has on several occasions had to "reverse-engineer a paper trail" to satisfy a counterparty's compliance review.

Source C, who has met the founder in a formal capacity on at least six occasions, describes him as "one of the few operators who reads the technical annexes himself". Source C says the founder has a reputation in the ministry for being blunt to the point of abrasiveness in licensing meetings, but that this has not, in his observation, translated into obstruction or evasion.

**2. Safety record and the 2021 incident**

Source A states that in the third quarter of 2021 a lifting operation on a support vessel chartered from Serra Azul Marítima resulted in a dropped load that struck deck plating some metres from two crew members. Source A says the event was logged internally as a high-potential near miss and closed out with a toolbox-talk action, and that in his view the energy involved and the proximity of personnel should have triggered notification to the maritime authority. Source A says he raised this with the founder and was told the matter was the vessel owner's to report.

Source B confirms an incident occurred in that period and that it was categorised as a near miss. She says the classification was made by the HSE director on the basis of the applicable matrix and was reviewed during the following year's external audit without adverse finding. Source B emphasises that the target's recordable incident frequency has fallen year-on-year since 2019 and that no lost-time injury has been recorded offshore since 2020.

Source C says the ministry holds no record of a reportable event attributable to the target in 2021, but cautions that vessel-side occurrences may sit with a different authority and would not necessarily surface in his files. He notes separately that the target's well-control drills were rated "adequate to good" in the most recent inspection cycle.

**3. Regulatory relationships and compliance record**

Source C states that Aurora Offshore Energia has twice been placed under enhanced monitoring — once in 2019 and once in 2022 — in both cases for late submission of environmental monitoring data rather than for the substance of the data. He says both episodes were resolved administratively, that no fine was levied on the second occasion, and that the company is not presently the subject of any sanction proceeding.

Source B corroborates the two episodes and attributes the 2022 delay to a change of environmental consultancy mid-cycle. She says the regulatory affairs function was expanded from three to nine people following that episode, and that the company now files ahead of deadline as a matter of policy. Source B denies any knowledge of facilitation payments or informal inducements in the licensing process and says the company's interactions with officials are minuted.

Source A is more sceptical, saying that in his time the company's approach to deadlines was "to ask forgiveness", though he too says he never saw or suspected improper payments to officials.

**4. Procurement integrity and supplier relationships**

Source D, who has run competitive processes in overlapping supply markets, says the target's tendering conduct is unusual in two respects: bid validity periods are very short, and the same two intermediary suppliers — she names Trimar Serviços Integrados and Nordeste Logística Offshore — appear repeatedly as winning counterparties on scopes that she would expect to attract six or more credible bidders. Source D stresses she has no visibility of the target's internal evaluation and offers this as a pattern observation only.

Source A links one of those suppliers to Renato Piscitelli, whom he describes as a former contracts manager at the target who left to establish an agency business and who retained an unusually direct line to the founder thereafter. Source A says he twice recommended competitive re-tendering of scopes held by that supplier and was overruled.

Source B says all sole-source awards above a defined threshold now require audit committee ratification and that a supplier due diligence programme was introduced in 2023. She was not able to comment on awards predating that programme.

**Assessment and outlook**

The reputational picture is mixed but not disqualifying. Technical and regulatory standing appear sound and improving; the founder's personal credibility with the ministry is an asset. The principal residual risks are historical rather than current: the classification of the 2021 lifting event, and the pre-2023 sole-source award pattern involving a supplier with a personal connection to the founder. Both are the kind of issue that would be uncomfortable in a post-acquisition audit rather than legally acute on present information.

**Gaps and next steps**

No source could speak to the target's non-Brazilian joint ventures. We recommend: (i) documentary review of the 2021 incident file and vessel owner's report; (ii) a spend-concentration analysis on the two named intermediaries for 2018–2023; (iii) corporate registry work on Trimar Serviços Integrados to test the alleged connection to Renato Piscitelli; and (iv) a further source with board-level visibility of related-party disclosure.
